vignette:
The first time she saw the code come over the hospital’s public address system, she didn’t flinch. It was just a sound, a sequence of tones and numbers that meant someone else’s emergency. Dr. Anae, fifty-eight, a psychiatrist on the consult-liaison service for the past twenty-two years, had heard that sound a thousand times. She knew what it meant: a life was slipping away, and a team was running to catch it. She never ran. Her job was to sit with the survivors afterward, to help them make sense of the aftermath.

That was before the bridge.

It was a Tuesday, six months ago. She was driving home from the hospital, the same coastal highway she had taken for two decades. The sky was a flat, gunmetal gray, and the sea below churned white against the rocks. She remembers the rain starting, a sudden, heavy curtain that blurred the windshield. She remembers slowing down, gripping the wheel with both hands. She remembers the sound of the truck’s air horn, the way it seemed to come from everywhere at once, and then the impact. A skid, a spin, the world tipping sideways. Her car hit the guardrail, tore through it, and hung there, suspended over the edge of the cliff, rocking gently in the wind.

She was upside down, held in by her seatbelt. The smell of gasoline was thick in the cabin. She could hear the rain on the metal, the tick of the engine cooling, and the groan of the car shifting on the twisted rail. She thought, very clearly, This is it. This is how I die. She thought of her son, who lived in Sydney and called her every Sunday. She thought of her ex-husband, and how they had parted without anger, just a quiet, mutual exhaustion. She thought of her patients, of all the people she had tried to help, and she felt a strange, hollow peace.

Then the rescue came. Firefighters, voices shouting, the screech of the Jaws of Life. She was pulled out, placed on a stretcher, and rushed to the same emergency room where she had consulted on hundreds of cases. She had a broken clavicle, three cracked ribs, and a deep laceration on her thigh. No internal bleeding. No traumatic brain injury. The doctors called her lucky. She heard the word and felt nothing.

She went back to work after six weeks. Her body had healed. She could walk without a limp. She could raise her arm above her head. But the world felt wrong. The first time she walked into the hospital cafeteria, the smell of antiseptic and burnt coffee hit her, and her heart began to pound so hard she thought she was having a heart attack. She had to sit down, put her head between her knees. A colleague asked if she was okay. She said she was fine. She said she was just tired.

She cannot drive the coastal highway anymore. She takes the inland route, which adds forty minutes to her commute. She tells herself it’s for the scenery. But she knows the truth: the moment she sees the ocean, she feels the car tipping, feels the seatbelt cutting into her chest, hears the groan of the metal. She will pull over, her hands shaking, and wait for the feeling to pass.

Her patients notice the change. She used to be a calm, steady presence, someone who could sit with the most agitated, dissociated, or suicidal patient and find a way to connect. Now, when a patient talks about a car accident, or a fall, or any moment when their life hung in the balance, she feels her own body respond. Her throat tightens. Her palms sweat. She has to consciously slow her breathing. She has started referring those cases to her younger colleagues. She tells herself it’s a matter of professional boundaries, that she needs to avoid countertransference. But she knows she is avoiding the echo of her own terror.

At night, she wakes up at 3:17 AM. Every single night. It is the exact time the ambulance arrived at the scene. She lies in the dark, her heart hammering, her mind replaying the sound of the truck’s horn. She does not dream of the accident. She dreams of the moment before it, of the flat gray sky, of the rain starting to fall. She wakes up already afraid.

She took the PCL-5 as part of a routine wellness screening for hospital staff. She scored a 37. She knows what that number means. She has administered the test to hundreds of patients. She knows the cutoff. She knows the diagnostic criteria. She knows she meets them. But she has not called a colleague. She has not made an appointment. She sits in her office, surrounded by the books she has read, the theories she has taught, the stories she has helped others rewrite. And she thinks, I am a psychiatrist. I should know how to fix this. But the car is still hanging over the edge, and she does not know how to get out.
